facts.claim: Change blindness can occur even in the absence of a visual disruption.
facts.quote: In two experiments, we demonstrate that change blindness can occur even in the absence of a visual disruption.

facts.claim: Subjects seldom noticed the switch [of pictures during a choice procedure], and in a post-test memory task, they also often remembered the manipulated choice as being their own.
facts.quote: Surprisingly, the subjects seldom noticed the switch, and in a post-test memory task, they also often remembered the manipulated choice as being their own.

facts.claim: When changes are sufficiently gradual, the visible change signal does not seem to draw attention, and large changes can go undetected.
facts.quote: When changes are sufficiently gradual, the visible change signal does not seem to draw attention, and large changes can go undetected.

facts.claim: People often fail to notice significant changes in visual scenes, even when these changes happen right in front of their eyes.
facts.quote: A large body of literature has shown that observers often fail to notice significant changes in visual scenes, even when these changes happen right in front of their eyes.

facts.claim: One of the major causes of change blindness for real-world objects is a lack of encoding time or attention to each object.
facts.quote: The results reported here suggest that one of the major causes of change blindness for real-world objects is a lack of encoding time or attention to each object

facts.claim: Increasing attention, the saliency of the changed object and spatial violations significantly reduce CB, specifically when measured using the real-world and film paradigms.
facts.quote: Increasing attention, the saliency of the changed object and spatial violations significantly reduce CB, specifically when measured using the real-world and film paradigms

research.angle: People often fail to notice large changes in their immediate environment due to a lack of attention or encoding time, even when those changes have consequences for their actions.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that people frequently fail to notice significant changes in scenes, though these failures can be mitigated by increased attention or saliency.
research.caveat: The research identifies various factors like encoding time, saliency, and the speed of change as critical variables that influence whether a change is actually perceived.
